title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite, eternal, and full of stars, why isn't every point in the night sky as bright as the sun?
summary: A simple observation — the sky goes dark at night — turns out to be one of the most powerful clues in the history of cosmology, ruling out an infinite, static, eternal universe long before anyone had proof the universe was expanding.
content:
It sounds too obvious to be a puzzle: the sky is dark at night because the sun has set. But astronomers as early as Johannes Kepler in 1610 noticed something stranger underneath that obvious fact. If the universe is infinite in extent, eternal in age, and roughly uniformly filled with stars, then no matter which direction you look, your line of sight should eventually hit the surface of a star — just as, standing in an infinitely large, evenly spaced forest, every line of sight eventually hits a tree trunk. If every point in the sky terminates on a stellar surface, then every point in the sky should shine with the average surface brightness of a star. The night sky should be a blaze of light, not black. This is Olbers' Paradox, popularized by Heinrich Olbers in 1823 though identified by several thinkers before him.

The naive fix that doesn't work

The first instinct is to say distant stars are dimmer, so their light fades before it reaches us. But this misses how geometry and brightness scale together. A star's apparent brightness falls off with the square of its distance — but the number of stars in a shell of space at that distance grows with the square of the distance too (more volume, more stars). The two effects exactly cancel. Each successive shell of the universe, however faint per star, contributes the same total amount of light as every closer shell. Sum infinitely many equal contributions and you get infinite brightness, not a fading twinkle. Distance alone cannot save the dark sky.

What actually resolves it

The real resolution is that the universe is not infinite in the way the paradox assumes — or more precisely, not infinitely old and infinitely luminous in every direction we can currently see. Light travels at a finite speed, and the universe has a finite age (about 13.8 billion years), so we can only receive light from stars close enough that their light has had time to reach us — the observable universe has a horizon. Stars beyond that horizon, even if they exist, haven't had their light arrive yet. Additionally, the universe is expanding, so light from very distant, very old sources is redshifted into wavelengths our eyes can't see — some of that ancient light is still arriving, just not as visible light: it shows up instead as the cosmic microwave background, the genuinely uniform faint glow that fills the entire sky at microwave wavelengths. In a real sense, Olbers was right that the sky isn't truly dark everywhere — it's just dark to human eyes.

A paradox that predicted the Big Bang before anyone believed in one

What makes Olbers' Paradox remarkable in hindsight is that it is a piece of naked-eye evidence against an infinite, static, eternal universe — the very cosmology most astronomers assumed by default for millennia. Centuries before Hubble measured galaxies receding from us, before Einstein's field equations, before anyone had a mechanism for a "beginning," the simple darkness of the night sky was already whispering that the universe must have a finite age or a finite reach, or both. Edgar Allan Poe, of all people, sketched an essentially correct qualitative resolution in his 1848 prose poem *Eureka*, arguing that light from the most distant stars simply hasn't reached us yet — intuiting a finite light-travel-time universe using nothing but reasoning, decades before it could be tested.

Why it still matters

Olbers' Paradox is a case study in how a childishly simple observation, taken seriously and followed rigorously, can constrain the deepest structure of reality. It's a reminder that cosmology doesn't only advance through telescopes and particle accelerators — sometimes it advances by someone asking "wait, why isn't this obvious thing true?" and refusing to accept a hand-wavy answer.

perspectives.title: Observational Astronomy Perspective
perspectives.description: The darkness of the night sky is itself a data point: it constrains how old, how large, and how densely populated with stars the observable universe can be.

perspectives.title: Cosmology Perspective
perspectives.description: A finite age of the universe combined with the finite speed of light creates a cosmic horizon — we simply haven't received light from stars beyond a certain distance yet, however many exist.

perspectives.title: Physics Perspective
perspectives.description: Cosmological redshift from universal expansion shifts ancient starlight out of the visible spectrum entirely, converting what would have been blinding ancient light into the invisible cosmic microwave background.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox was informally solved by a poet, Edgar Allan Poe, using pure reasoning about finite light-travel time decades before Hubble's observations gave cosmologists the tools to confirm it.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Olbers' Paradox shows how a contradiction between a simple theoretical model (infinite static universe) and a mundane everyday observation (dark sky) can falsify a cosmological worldview without any specialized instruments.

openQuestions: What lies beyond the observable universe's horizon, and will we ever be able to know?
Could there be structure or light sources bright enough to still challenge our resolution of the paradox in ways we haven't considered?
How many other 'obvious' everyday observations are secretly powerful constraints on cosmology that no one has thought to formalize?
As the universe continues expanding, will the night sky grow darker still over cosmic time?
